notes.title: Introduction to Euclid's Geometry — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Introduction
The study of Euclid's Geometry is the foundation of all mathematical reasoning and proof. Understanding these basic axioms and postulates is crucial as they form the logical building blocks for more complex geometry you will study in higher classes and is frequently tested in exams.

### Euclid's Axioms
Euclid proposed certain common notions or axioms that were considered self-evident truths requiring no proof. These are universal statements that apply to all branches of mathematics. For instance, one of his most famous axioms is that "things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another." These axioms form the starting point for any logical deduction in geometry.

### Euclid's Postulates
Unlike axioms, Euclid's postulates are specific to geometry and are the basic assumptions from which he derived other geometric propositions. He gave five main postulates. The most famous of these is the fifth postulate, also known as the parallel postulate, which states that if a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, the two straight lines, if produced indefinitely, meet on that side on which the angles are less than the two right angles.

### Definitions
Before proving any theorem, Euclid started with clear definitions of basic geometric terms. He defined a point as "that which has no part," a line as "a breadthless length," and a plane surface as "a surface which lies evenly with the straight lines on itself." These definitions, while simple, are essential for understanding the objects we are working with.

### The Five Postulates in Detail
Let's look at the five postulates more closely. The first postulate states that a straight line can be drawn from any one point to any other point. The second says that a terminated line can be produced indefinitely. The third postulate allows us to describe a circle with any centre and radius. The fourth states that all right angles are equal to one another. The fifth postulate, as mentioned, is about the properties of parallel lines.

### Equivalent Versions of the Fifth Postulate
The fifth postulate is so significant that it has several equivalent versions. One of the most famous equivalent statements is Playfair's Axiom, which says that "given a line and a point not on it, exactly one line can be drawn through the point that is parallel to the given line." This version is often easier to understand and work with than the original statement.

## Example
Let's use the first postulate to solve a simple problem. The problem states: Given two points A and B, 5 cm apart, construct a line segment AB. Using the first postulate, which says a straight line can be drawn from any point to any other point, we can use a ruler to draw a straight line connecting point A and point B, ensuring the distance between them is 5 cm. This simple act is a direct application of one of Euclid's most fundamental postulates.

## Quick Revision
- Euclid's Geometry is based on axioms, postulates, and definitions.
- Axioms are universal truths applicable to all mathematics.
- Postulates are specific assumptions for geometry.
- The fifth postulate is about the properties of parallel lines.
- Playfair's Axiom is an easier version of the fifth postulate.
- A point, line, and plane are the basic undefined terms in geometry.
- Euclid wrote a book called 'Elements' which contained all these principles.
- The logical structure of starting from basic assumptions is called a deductive system.

## Exam Tips
- Always state the axiom or postulate you are using in your proof to show logical clarity.
- Understand the difference between an axiom and a postulate clearly, as questions often test this distinction.
- The fifth postulate and its equivalent versions (like Playfair's Axiom) are high-weightage topics, so focus on them.
- Practice drawing diagrams based on the postulates, as visual understanding is often tested.
- Avoid memorizing definitions word-for-word; instead, understand the meaning and explain them in your own words for better marks.

notes.title: पत्र व निबंध लेखन (Writing) — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## पत्र व निबंध लेखन नोट्स

पत्र और निबंध लेखन हिंदी विषय का एक बहुत महत्वपूर्ण अध्याय है, जो आपके बोर्ड परीक्षा में अक्सर 10-15 अंकों का विशेष योगदान देता है। यह अध्याय आपको वास्तविक जीवन की स्थितियों में आवश्यक संचार कौशल सिखाता है और आपके भाषा विकास में मदद करता है।

### पत्र लेखन की संरचना
किसी भी प्रकार के पत्र लिखते समय इसकी एक निश्चित संरचना होती है। पहले आप पत्र के ऊपर बाएँ कोने में अपना पता और फिर दाएँ कोने में दिनांक लिखते हैं। इसके बाद पत्र के शीर्षक के नीचे संबोधित व्यक्ति का पता आता है। पत्र का मुख्य भाग तीन भागों में बाँटा जाता है- प्रारंभ, मुख्य भाग और समापन। अंत में आप अपना नाम और उस व्यक्ति का नाम लिखते हैं जिसे पत्र लिखा जा रहा है।

### पत्र के प्रकार
पत्र कई प्रकार के हो सकते हैं जैसे निजी पत्र, आधिकारिक पत्र, व्यावसायिक पत्र और प्रशंसा पत्र। निजी पत्र में आप अपने दोस्त या परिवार के सदस्यों से बात करते हैं और भाषा सरल और आरामदायक होती है। आधिकारिक पत्र विभागों या किसी अधिकारी को लिखे जाते हैं, जिनमें भाषा और शैली बहुत औपचारिक और सुसंगत होती है।

### निबंध लेखन की रूपरेखा
एक अच्छा निबंध लिखने के लिए सबसे पहले आपको विषय पर विचार करना चाहिए। फिर एक सुसंगत रूपरेखा तैयार करें जिसमें प्रारंभ, मध्य और अंत तीन भाग हों। प्रारंभ में आप विषय का परिचय देते हैं। मध्य भाग में आप अपने विचारों को तर्कों और उदाहरणों के साथ विस्तार से लिखते हैं। अंत में आप अपने विचारों का सारांश देते हैं और एक निष्कर्ष प्रस्तुत करते हैं।

### भाषा और शैली
जब आप पत्र या निबंध लिखते हैं, तो भाषा साफ, सरल और विचारों को व्यक्त करने में प्रभावी होनी चाहिए। लंबे और जटिल वाक्यों से बचें। अपने विचारों को तर्कसंगत और व्यवस्थित ढंग से प्रस्तुत करें। उस शैली का प्रयोग करें जो लेखन के प्रकार के अनुरूप हो। उदाहरण के लिए, एक निबंध में आप अपनी राय व्यक्त कर सकते हैं, लेकिन एक आधिकारिक पत्र में आप बहुत औपचारिक और तटस्थ भाषा का प्रयोग करेंगे।

### गलतियों से बचाव
पत्र और निबंध लिखते समय वर्तनी और व्याकरण की गलतियों से बचना बहुत जरूरी है। लिखने के बाद अवश्य अपने लेखन को दोबारा पढ़ें। सुनिश्चित करें कि पत्र का पता और दिनांक सही है। निबंध में विषय से बाहर के विचार न लाएं। अपने विचारों को अलग-अलग अनुच्छेदों में लिखने से पाठक को समझने में आसानी होगी।

## उदाहरण
एक दोस्त को पत्र लिखना:  
मेरा प्रिय राज,  
तुम्हारा पता:  
राज शर्मा,  
बी-42, सेक्टर-15,  
नोएडा।  
दिनांक: 15 अक्टूबर, 2023  
प्रिय राज,  
कैसे हो तुम? यहाँ सब ठीक है। मैं अपनी छुट्टियों का आनंद ले रहा हूँ। मैंने इस सप्ताह लखनऊ जाने की योजना बनाई है। वहाँ के बाजारों और स्थानों को देखना मेरा लंबे समय से चाहा था। क्या तुम भी आना चाहोगे? यदि हाँ, तो मुझे जल्द बताओ।  
तुम्हारा मित्र,  
अजय।

## त्वरित समीक्षा
- पत्र लेखन में भाषा औपचारिक और सरल होनी चाहिए।
- निबंध में विषय का परिचय, विस्तार और निष्कर्ष होता है।
- पत्र के भाग हैं: पता, दिनांक, संबोधन, मुख्य भाग और अंतिम शब्द।
- निबंध लिखने से पहले रूपरेखा बनाएं।
- वर्तनी और व्याकरण की गलतियों से बचें।
- अपने विचारों को तर्कों और उदाहरणों से समझाएं।
- पत्र का शब्दावली उस व्यक्ति के अनुरूप हो जिसे पत्र लिखा जा रहा है।

## परीक्षा सलाह
- पहले पत्र के प्रकार को समझें और उसके अनुसार भाषा चुनें।
- निबंध में विषय से बाहर जाने से बचें, यह नकारात्मक अंक देने का कारण बन सकता है।
- लिखने के बाद अवश्य अपने लेखन को एक बार फिर से पढ़ें और सुधार करें।
- बार-बार इस्तेमाल होने वाले शब्दों के स्थान पर नए शब्दों का प्रयोग करें।
- विशेष रूप से निबंध के लिए एक अच्छा शीर्षक चुनें, यह पहली छाप बनाता है।

notes.title: काव्य खंड (Poetry) — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## काव्य खंड (Poetry)

काव्य खंड वह महत्वपूर्ण अध्याय है जो आपको कविता के अंतर्गत आने वाली विभिन्न छोटी विधाओं से परिचित कराता है। यह अध्याय आपके लिखित परीक्षाओं में अंक लाने के लिए बेहद उपयोगी है क्योंकि इसमें कविताओं के माध्यम से व्यावहारिक ज्ञान दिया गया है और इसके प्रश्न अक्सर आते हैं।

### कविता की परिभाषा और विशेषताएं
कविता एक ऐसी साहित्यिक विधा है जिसमें भावों को गद्य की अपेक्षा अधिक सुंदर, गीतात्मक और संक्षिप्त रूप में प्रस्तुत किया जाता है। इसकी सबसे बड़ी विशेषता गद्य की तुलना में अधिक छंद और लय होती है। कविता में लेखक अपने भावों, विचारों और कल्पनाओं को रंगीन शब्दों के माध्यम से व्यक्त करता है ताकि पाठक उसे आसानी से समझ और महसूस कर सके।

### खंड का अर्थ और प्रकार
खंड का अर्थ है किसी बड़े ग्रंथ का एक छोटा अंश या भाग। काव्य खंड का अर्थ है किसी बड़ी कविता का एक ऐसा अंश जो स्वयं में पूर्ण हो और किसी विशेष भाव या विचार को व्यक्त करे। यह कविता का एक छोटा, पूर्ण और स्वतंत्र टुकड़ा होता है जिसमें एक निश्चित भाव या कथा होती है।

### खंड की भाषा और शैली
खंड में प्रयुक्त भाषा सरल, स्पष्ट और भावपूर्ण होती है। यह शब्दों का चुनाव बहुत ध्यान से किया जाता है ताकि वे भावों को बल मिले। शैली का ध्यान रखा जाता है कि वह पाठक के मन पर गहरा प्रभाव डाले। कभी-कभी खंड में गद्य के तत्व भी मिल जाते हैं जो इसे और अधिक रोचक बना देते हैं।

### खंड में भाव और अनुभूति
खंड का मुख्य आधार भाव होता है। यह किसी एक भाव जैसे प्रेम, वीरता, प्रकृति, देशभक्ति या किसी व्यक्तिगत अनुभव को केंद्र में रखकर लिखा जाता है। पाठक इसे पढ़ते हुए उस भाव का सहानुभूति से अनुभव करता है और लेखक की दुनिया में खुद को खो जाता है।

### खंड का महत्व और प्रभाव
खंड का महत्व इस बात में है कि यह पाठक को बड़ी कविता को पढ़ने के बिना भी उसके सार को समझने में मदद करता है। यह छोटे आकार में भी बड़ा प्रभाव डालता है। खंड का प्रभाव इतना गहरा होता है कि वह पाठक के मन में लंबे समय तक बना रहता है और उसके विचारों और व्यवहार को प्रभावित करता है।

## उदाहरण
आप अपनी पुस्तक में दिए गए किसी भी खंड को ले सकते हैं। उदाहरण के लिए, यदि खंड में प्रकृति का वर्णन है, तो आप उसमें प्रयुक्त 'हरियाली', 'सुगंध', 'वायु' जैसे शब्दों पर ध्यान दें। इन शब्दों के माध्यम से लेखक ने प्रकृति की सुंदरता का एक संपूर्ण चित्र बनाया है, जो हमारे मन को आकर्षित करता है।

## त्वरित समीक्षा
- काव्य खंड एक पूर्ण और स्वतंत्र कविता का छोटा अंश है।
- इसमें एक विशेष भाव या विचार केंद्र में होता है।
- इसकी भाषा सरल, स्पष्ट और भावपूर्ण होती है।
- खंड पाठक पर गहरा और लंबे समय तक चलने वाला प्रभाव डालता है।
- यह गद्य और पद्य के तत्वों का सुंदर संगम हो सकता है।
- खंड में लेखक की व्यक्तिगत अनुभूतियां छिपी होती हैं।

## परीक्षा योग्य बिंदु
- परीक्षा में खंड से संबंधित प्रश्नों को अच्छी तरह समझने के लिए उसे ध्यानपूर्वक पढ़ें।
- खंड में आए गए महत्वपूर्ण शब्दों और उनके अर्थों को याद करें।
- खंड का मुख्य भाव और उसका पाठक पर पड़ने वाला प्रभाव समझें।
- अपने शब्दों में खंड का सार लिखने का अभ्यास करें। यह आपको अंक लाने में मदद करेगा।
- खंड की रचनात्मक विशेषताओं का विश्लेषण करने का प्रयास करें, यह अच्छे अंक दिला सकता है।

notes.title: गद्य खंड (Prose) — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## गद्य खंड (प्रौढ़ गद्य)

गद्य खंड अध्याय आपको विभिन्न प्रकार के गद्य रचनाओं से परिचित कराता है, जो आपके भाषा बोध और लेखन कौशल को निखारने में महत्वपूर्ण भूमिका निभाता है। यह अध्याय आपको अपने विचारों को व्यवस्थित और स्पष्ट रूप से प्रस्तुत करने में मदद करता है, जो बोर्ड परीक्षाओं में निबंध लेखन और व्याकरण से संबंधित प्रश्नों के लिए अत्यंत आवश्यक है।

### गद्य की परिभाषा और विशेषताएँ
गद्य वह साहित्यिक विधा है जिसमें कथा, वर्णन, तर्क या विचारों को गद्यात्मक रूप से, अर्थात् सामान्य बोलचाल की भाषा में, प्रस्तुत किया जाता है। इसकी विशेषताएँ यह हैं कि इसमें वाक्य लंबे हो सकते हैं, विचार विकसित होते हैं और लेखक अपने विचारों को पूरी गहनता से व्यक्त कर सकता है।

### गद्य और पद्य का भेद
गद्य और पद्य दोनों ही साहित्य के रूप हैं, लेकिन उनके बीच एक मूलभूत अंतर है। पद्य छंदों में लिखा जाता है और उसमें लय, गति तथा अलंकारों का प्रयोग होता है। दूसरी ओर, गद्य गद्यात्मक रूप में होता है, जो वास्तविकता को सीधे और स्पष्ट ढंग से व्यक्त करता है।

### गद्य के प्रकार
गद्य कई प्रकार के हो सकते हैं, जैसे कि वर्णनात्मक गद्य (किसी व्यक्ति, स्थान या घटना का विस्तृत वर्णन), कथात्मक गद्य (किसी कहानी या घटना का वृत्तांत), तथा विचारात्मक गद्य (किसी विषय पर गहन चिंतन और तर्क)। प्रत्येक प्रकार का अपना एक विशिष्ट शैली और उद्देश्य होता है।

### गद्य रचना के तत्व
एक अच्छी गद्य रचना के कुछ महत्वपूर्ण तत्व होते हैं। इनमें विषय की व्यापकता, भाषा की सरलता और स्पष्टता, तथा विचारों की व्यवस्थित प्रस्तुति शामिल हैं। एक अच्छी गद्य रचना पाठक को आकर्षित करती है और उसे लेखक के विचारों तक पहुँचने में सहायता करती है।

## उदाहरण
आप अपने दैनिक जीवन का अनुभव लेकर एक छोटा गद्य लिख सकते हैं। उदाहरण के लिए, आप अपने स्कूल के एक दिन का वर्णन कर सकते हैं। इसमें आप अपने स्कूल के वातावरण, अध्यापकों के साथ अनुभव, और दोस्तों के साथ मज़े का वर्णन करें। इस तरह का लेखन आपको वर्णनात्मक गद्य की रचना करने में मदद करेगा।

## त्वरित समीक्षा
- गद्य एक ऐसा साहित्यिक रूप है जो गद्यात्मक भाषा में लिखा जाता है।
- गद्य और पद्य का मुख्य भेद छंदों की उपस्थिति में है।
- गद्य के विभिन्न प्रकार होते हैं जैसे वर्णनात्मक, कथात्मक और विचारात्मक।
- एक अच्छी गद्य रचना के लिए स्पष्टता और व्यवस्थित विचारों की आवश्यकता होती है।
- गद्य रचना में भाषा की सरलता और प्रवाह प्रमुख होता है।
- इस अध्याय से आपको भाषा की बारीकियों की समझ बढ़ेगी।

## परीक्षा योग्य बिंदु
- गद्य और पद्य में अंतर समझें और इसे अपने शब्दों में लिखें।
- अपनी पाठ्यपुस्तक की गद्य रचनाओं के विषय, भाव और शैली पर ध्यान दें।
- विभिन्न प्रकार के गद्य (वर्णनात्मक, कथात्मक) के उदाहरण दें।
- किसी भी विषय पर एक छोटा गद्य लिखने का अभ्यास करें, जो आपको निबंध लेखन में फायदा देगा।
- परीक्षा में गद्य से संबंधित प्रश्नों का उत्तर सरल और स्पष्ट भाषा में दें।

notes.title: व्याकरण (Grammar) — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## व्याकरण (Grammar) - विशेष रूप से वाक्य के अंग

व्याकरण हिंदी भाषा का एक बहुत ही महत्वपूर्ण अंग है। इसके बिना हमारी बातचीत और लेखन अधूरा रह जाता है। बोर्ड परीक्षाओं में व्याकरण से सीधे-सीधे प्रश्न पूछे जाते हैं और यह आपके निबंध लेखन को भी बेहतर बनाता है।

### वाक्य का अर्थ और परिभाषा
वाक्य एक ऐसी शब्द-समूह होता है जिसमें किसी पूरे अर्थ को व्यक्त करने वाले शब्द होते हैं और उस पर एक पूर्ण विचार टिका रहता है। वाक्य में एक से अधिक वाक्यांश हो सकते हैं और उसमें सदैव एक क्रिया अवश्य मिलती है।

### वाक्य के अंग
वाक्य के मुख्य दो अंग होते हैं: कर्ता और क्रिया। कर्ता वह होता है जो कार्य करता है और क्रिया वह कार्य होता है जो कर्ता द्वारा किया जाता है। उदाहरण के लिए, 'राम खाता है' में 'राम' कर्ता और 'खाता है' क्रिया है।

### कर्ता के भेद
कर्ता को दो प्रकार में बाँटा गया है: सकर्मक कर्ता और अकर्मक कर्ता। सकर्मक कर्ता के कार्य से कोई अन्य वस्तु प्रभावित होती है, जैसे 'राम पत्र लिखता है' (यहाँ पत्र प्रभावित हुआ)। अकर्मक कर्ता के कार्य से कोई अन्य वस्तु प्रभावित नहीं होती, जैसे 'राम चलता है' (कोई अन्य वस्तु प्रभावित नहीं हुई)।

### क्रिया के भेद
क्रिया भी दो प्रकार की होती है: सकर्मक क्रिया और अकर्मक क्रिया। सकर्मक क्रिया किसी कर्म का बोध कराती है और उसके बाद कर्म आता है, जैसे 'मैं पुस्तक पढ़ता हूँ' (यहाँ 'पढ़ता हूँ' सकर्मक क्रिया है और 'पुस्तक' कर्म है)। अकर्मक क्रिया का सीधा संबंध कर्ता से होता है और उसके बाद कर्म नहीं आता, जैसे 'बच्चा रोता है'।

### वाक्य के प्रकार
वाक्य के अर्थ और उद्देश्य के आधार पर उन्हें चार मुख्य प्रकारों में बाँटा गया है: विधानवाचक, प्रश्नवाचक, निषेधवाचक और आज्ञावाचक। विधानवाचक वाक्य किसी बात का वर्णन करता है, प्रश्नवाचक किसी बात के बारे में पूछता है, निषेधवाचक किसी बात का खंडन करता है और आज्ञावाचक किसी को कुछ करने के लिए कहता है।

## त्वरित याद करें
- वाक्य में हमेशा एक पूर्ण अर्थ होता है।
- कर्ता कार्य करने वाला होता है।
- क्रिया कार्य या क्रिया-विशेष होती है।
- सकर्मक कर्ता का कर्म होता है।
- अकर्मक क्रिया का कर्म नहीं होता।
- चार मुख्य वाक्य प्रकार हैं: विधान, प्रश्न, निषेध, आज्ञा।

## परीक्षा योग्य टिप्स
- वाक्य के अंग और उनके भेद पर ध्यान दें, यह सबसे अधिक पूछे जाने वाले प्रश्न हैं।
- सकर्मक और अकर्मक कर्ता-क्रिया को समझने के लिए उदाहरण ज़रूर देखें।
- वाक्य के प्रकारों को अलग-अलग समझकर उनके उदाहरण याद रखें।
- व्याकरण के नियमों को याद करने के बजाय उन्हें अपने लेखन में लागू करने का अभ्यास करें।

notes.title: Linear Equations in Two Variables — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Linear Equations in Two Variables

This chapter is a fundamental building block in algebra, forming the basis for coordinate geometry and is frequently tested in exams. Understanding how to solve and graph these equations will help you in almost all future topics in mathematics.

### What is a Linear Equation in Two Variables?
A linear equation in two variables is an equation that can be written in the form `ax + by + c = 0`, where `a`, `b`, and `c` are real numbers, and both `a` and `b` are not zero at the same time. The letters `x` and `y` represent the two variables, and the highest power of both variables is one. This means their graphs will always be straight lines.

### Solutions of an Equation
The solution to a linear equation in two variables is a pair of values for `x` and `y` that make the equation true. Unlike in one variable, there isn't just one solution; in fact, there are infinitely many solutions. These solutions can be represented as ordered pairs `(x, y)`, which you can later plot on a graph to form the line that represents the equation.

### Graphical Representation
The graphical representation of a linear equation in two variables is always a straight line. Every point on this line is a solution to the equation. To draw this line, you only need two points. The easiest points to find are usually the intercepts, where the line crosses the x-axis and y-axis.

### Finding Intercepts
The x-intercept is the point where the line crosses the x-axis. At this point, the value of `y` is zero. To find it, simply substitute `y = 0` into the equation and solve for `x`. Similarly, the y-intercept is the point where the line crosses the y-axis. Here, the value of `x` is zero, so you substitute `x = 0` and solve for `y`.

### Equations of Lines Parallel to Axes
There are two special cases of linear equations. The first is an equation like `x = a`, which represents a straight line parallel to the y-axis. The second is an equation like `y = b`, which represents a straight line parallel to the x-axis. These are not in the standard `ax + by + c = 0` form but are still linear equations.

### Graphical Method of Solution
To solve a system of two linear equations graphically, you draw the lines for both equations on the same graph. The point where the two lines intersect gives the solution to the system of equations. If the lines are parallel, they never intersect, meaning there is no solution. If the lines coincide (are the same line), there are infinitely many solutions.

## Example
Let's find the intercepts and graph the equation `2x + 3y = 6`.
*   **To find the x-intercept:** Set `y = 0`.
    `2x + 3(0) = 6`
    `2x = 6`
    `x = 3`. The x-intercept is (3, 0).
*   **To find the y-intercept:** Set `x = 0`.
    `2(0) + 3y = 6`
    `3y = 6`
    `y = 2`. The y-intercept is (0, 2).
Now, plot the points (3, 0) and (0, 2) on a graph sheet and draw a straight line passing through them. This line is the graphical representation of the equation.

## Quick Revision
*   A linear equation in two variables has the form `ax + by + c = 0`.
*   It has infinitely many solutions, represented as ordered pairs `(x, y)`.
*   The graph of a linear equation is always a straight line.
*   The x-intercept is found by setting `y = 0`.
*   The y-intercept is found by setting `x = 0`.
*   The solution to a system of two equations is their point of intersection.
*   Parallel lines have no solution, and coincident lines have infinite solutions.

## Exam Tips
*   **Always find two points:** To draw a line, you must find at least two points. Using the intercepts is the easiest and most reliable method.
*   **Check your work:** After finding a solution, substitute the values of `x` and `y` back into the original equation to verify if it satisfies the equation.
*   **Be careful with signs:** A common mistake is to mess up the signs while shifting terms from one side of the equation to the other. Do it step-by-step to avoid errors.
*   **Focus on graphical questions:** Questions asking you to draw the line and find the solution graphically often carry good marks. Practice plotting points and drawing neat lines.
keyPoints: A linear equation in two variables has the form `ax + by + c = 0`.
It has infinitely many solutions, represented as ordered pairs `(x, y)`.
The graph of a linear equation is always a straight line.
The x-intercept is found by setting `y = 0`.
The y-intercept is found by setting `x = 0`.
The solution to a system of two equations is their point of intersection.
Parallel lines have no solution, and coincident lines have infinite solutions.

notes.title: Coordinate Geometry — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Coordinate Geometry is a crucial chapter in Class 9 Maths as it introduces the foundation for plotting points and understanding their relationship, which is essential for higher-level mathematics and real-world applications like mapping and computer graphics.

### Cartesian Plane
The Cartesian plane is a two-dimensional surface formed by two perpendicular number lines, the horizontal x-axis and the vertical y-axis, that intersect at a point called the origin (0,0). This grid allows us to locate any point in the plane using a pair of numbers known as coordinates.

### Coordinates of a Point
Every point on the plane has a unique address called an ordered pair (x, y), where 'x' is the distance along the x-axis (abscissa) and 'y' is the distance along the y-axis (ordinate). The first number in the pair tells you how far to move horizontally from the origin, and the second number tells you how far to move vertically.

### Plotting Points
To plot a point, you start at the origin, move horizontally according to the x-coordinate (right for positive, left for negative), and then move vertically according to the y-coordinate (up for positive, down for negative). The intersection of these two movements is the exact location of the point on the plane.

### Quadrants
The two axes divide the Cartesian plane into four regions called quadrants, numbered counter-clockwise from the top-right as I, II, III, and IV. The signs of the coordinates change in each quadrant: (+, +) in I, (-, +) in II, (-, -) in III, and (+, -) in IV.

### Distance from Origin
The distance of a point (x, y) from the origin (0,0) can be found using the Pythagorean theorem, which gives the formula √(x² + y²). This calculates the length of the straight line connecting the point to the origin, forming the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle.

## Example
Let's plot the point (-3, 2). We start at the origin (0,0). Since the x-coordinate is -3, we move 3 units to the left along the x-axis. From there, since the y-coordinate is 2, we move 2 units up. The point where we land is (-3, 2), which is located in the second quadrant.

## Quick Revision
- The Cartesian plane is formed by x-axis and y-axis intersecting at the origin.
- An ordered pair (x, y) gives the exact location of a point.
- The x-coordinate (abscissa) is horizontal, and the y-coordinate (ordinate) is vertical.
- Quadrants are numbered I to IV counter-clockwise, with specific sign patterns.
- The distance of a point (x, y) from the origin is √(x² + y²).
- Points on the x-axis have a y-coordinate of 0.
- Points on the y-axis have an x-coordinate of 0.
- The origin has coordinates (0, 0).

## Exam Tips
- Always label your axes and the origin clearly when plotting points to avoid confusion and earn full marks.
- Pay close attention to the signs of the coordinates, as they determine the correct quadrant for the point.
- Remember the rule of thumb: for the x-coordinate, you move left/right, and for the y-coordinate, you move up/down.
- Practice plotting multiple points on the same graph to build confidence and speed, as this is a common question type.
- When calculating distance from the origin, be careful with squaring negative numbers, as a negative number squared becomes positive.

An ordered pair (x, y) gives the exact location of a point.
The x-coordinate (abscissa) is horizontal, and the y-coordinate (ordinate) is vertical.
Quadrants are numbered I to IV counter-clockwise, with specific sign patterns.
The distance of a point (x, y) from the origin is √(x² + y²).
Points on the x-axis have a y-coordinate of 0.
Points on the y-axis have an x-coordinate of 0.
The origin has coordinates (0, 0).

notes.title: Writing Skills & Grammar — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Introduction
Writing Skills & Grammar is a foundational chapter that forms the backbone of your English studies. Mastering this chapter is crucial not only for scoring well in your board exams but also for developing clear and effective communication skills that will benefit you throughout your life.

### Parts of Speech
Parts of Speech are the eight categories into which words are classified based on their function in a sentence. These categories include Nouns (names of people, places, or things), Verbs (action words), Adjectives (describing words), Adverbs (words describing verbs or adjectives), Pronouns (words that replace nouns), Prepositions (words showing the relationship between nouns), Conjunctions (words connecting clauses or sentences), and Interjections (words expressing sudden emotions). Understanding these is the first step to analyzing any sentence.

### Tenses
Tenses indicate the time of an action—whether it is happening in the present, happened in the past, or will happen in the future. The three main tenses are Present, Past, and Future, each of which has four forms: Simple, Continuous, Perfect, and Perfect Continuous. For instance, the simple present tense is used for habitual actions ("I go to school"), while the past continuous describes an action that was ongoing at a specific time in the past ("I was reading when he arrived").

### Active and Passive Voice
The active voice is used when the subject of the sentence performs the action (e.g., "The dog chased the cat"). In contrast, the passive voice is used when the subject receives the action, and the focus is on the action itself rather than who performed it (e.g., "The cat was chased by the dog"). While the active voice is generally more direct and preferred in writing, the passive voice is useful when the doer of the action is unknown or irrelevant.

### Reported Speech
Reported Speech, also known as Indirect Speech, is used to convey what someone else has said without using their exact words. It involves changing the pronouns, tenses, and sometimes the word order to fit the new context. For example, the direct speech "He said, 'I am happy'" becomes "He said that he was happy" in reported speech. This skill is essential for summarizing conversations and narratives.

### Modals
Modal auxiliary verbs, or modals, are special helping verbs that add meaning to the main verb. They express ideas like necessity (must, should), possibility (may, might), ability (can, could), and permission (may, can). Unlike other verbs, they do not change their form for different subjects and are followed by the base form of the main verb, as in "You should finish your homework."

## Example
**Change the following sentence into the passive voice:** "The chef prepares a delicious meal every day."
**Solution:** In the passive voice, the object of the active sentence ("a delicious meal") becomes the subject. The verb "prepares" is changed to its past participle form "prepared," and "by the chef" is added to indicate the doer.
**Passive Voice:** "A delicious meal is prepared by the chef every day."

## Quick Revision
- A sentence must have a subject and a predicate to be complete.
- **Subject-Verb Agreement** ensures that the verb matches the subject in number (singular/plural).
- A **clause** is a group of words with a subject and predicate, while a **phrase** is a group of words without a subject and predicate.
- **Conjunctions** like 'and', 'but', and 'or' are used to join words, phrases, or clauses.
- Punctuation marks like the full stop, comma, and question mark are essential for clarity and correct sentence structure.
- **Prepositions** show the relationship between a noun/pronoun and other words in a sentence (e.g., in, on, at, for).

## Exam Tips
- Always read the question carefully, especially in grammar exercises, as a single word can change the entire requirement.
- For writing tasks, plan your answer with a short outline before you begin to ensure your ideas are well-organized and you don't forget any key points.
- Pay special attention to common errors like subject-verb agreement and the correct use of tenses, as these are frequently tested.
- In reported speech questions, remember to shift the tense back one step and adjust pronouns and time expressions accordingly.

A **clause** is a group of words with a subject and predicate, while a **phrase** is a group of words without a subject and predicate.

notes.title: Literature – Prose — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Introduction
The prose chapter in your Class 9 English syllabus is a cornerstone for developing your analytical and interpretive skills. Mastering these stories and essays is crucial, as they form the basis for a significant portion of your final exam questions, testing both your understanding and your ability to express it clearly.

### Character Analysis
A character is not just a name in a story; they are the driving force behind the plot and the primary vehicle for the author's message. To analyze a character, you must look beyond their actions and consider their motivations, their internal conflicts, and how they change (or don't change) from the beginning to the end of the narrative. Ask yourself what the author is trying to show us about human nature through this character.

### Setting and Atmosphere
The setting of a story is more than just the time and place where it happens; it is the world the author creates for the reader. The atmosphere is the mood or feeling that this world evokes. A dark, stormy night can create a sense of fear and suspense, while a bright, sunny morning might suggest hope and new beginnings. Understanding how the setting influences the characters and the plot is key to a deep comprehension of the text.

### Central Theme
The central theme is the underlying message or the main idea that the author wants to convey through the story. It is often a universal truth about life, society, or human emotions. A theme isn't stated directly; it's something you have to infer by looking at the characters, the plot, and the conflicts they face. Common themes in prose include love, loss, justice, courage, and the conflict between tradition and modernity.

### Narrative Perspective
The perspective from which a story is told is called the narrative point of view. It can be first-person (using "I"), where we experience the story through one character's limited viewpoint, or third-person (using "he/she/they"), where the narrator is outside the story. The choice of perspective is deliberate; it controls how much information the reader gets and shapes our understanding of the characters and events.

### Plot and Structure
The plot is the sequence of events that make up the story, usually built around a conflict. It typically follows a structure: exposition (introduction of characters and setting), rising action (events that build tension), climax (the turning point or most intense moment), falling action (events after the climax), and resolution (the conclusion). Recognizing this structure helps you follow the author's storytelling logic and understand how the story builds to its conclusion.

## Example
Imagine a story where a young boy, Rohan, is torn between his love for his grandmother's traditional folk tales and his friends' obsession with modern video games. The rising action involves Rohan secretly borrowing his grandmother's old storybook. The climax occurs when he gets caught and must choose between defending his passion or giving in to peer pressure. The central theme here could be the struggle between **preserving cultural heritage** and **conforming to modern trends**.

## Quick Revision
- A character's **motivation** is the "why" behind their actions.
- The **setting** directly influences the **atmosphere** and mood of the story.
- The central theme is the author's underlying **message** about life.
- The **narrative perspective** determines how much the reader knows.
- The plot's structure is built around a central **conflict**.
- The **climax** is the story's most intense turning point.
- The **resolution** provides closure to the central conflict.

## Exam Tips
- Always support your answers with specific **examples** or quotes from the text to earn higher marks.
- Pay close attention to the **title** of the prose piece; it often gives a crucial clue to the central theme.
- When answering questions about characters, focus on their **development** throughout the story, not just their initial description.
- Manage your time wisely; questions on prose often require longer, more descriptive answers, so allocate time accordingly to ensure you attempt all parts of the question paper.

The **setting** directly influences the **atmosphere** and mood of the story.
The central theme is the author's underlying **message** about life.
The **narrative perspective** determines how much the reader knows.
The plot's structure is built around a central **conflict**.
The **climax** is the story's most intense turning point.
The **resolution** provides closure to the central conflict.

notes.title: Literature – Poetry — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Introduction
Poetry is a beautiful and vital part of your English curriculum, helping you appreciate language in its most artistic form. Mastering this chapter is crucial not just for scoring well in your exams, but also for developing a deeper understanding of human emotions, imagery, and expression.

### The Essence of Poetry
Poetry is a form of literature that uses aesthetic and rhythmic qualities of language, such as **phonaesthetics** and **meter**, to evoke meanings in addition to, or in place of, the prosaic ostensible meaning. It's the art of crafting language to express feelings, ideas, or stories in a condensed and powerful way, often using devices like metaphors and similes.

### Imagery and Sensory Language
Imagery is the use of vivid and descriptive language that appeals to the five senses: sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch. A poet uses sensory details to create a mental picture in the reader's mind, making the experience more immersive and emotionally resonant. For example, describing the "crunch of autumn leaves" or the "sweet scent of rain on hot earth" are forms of imagery.

### Figures of Speech
These are tools poets use to create special effects and add interest to their writing. Common figures of speech include **metaphors** (a direct comparison between two unlike things), **similes** (a comparison using "like" or "as"), and **personification** (giving human qualities to inanimate objects). These devices help simplify complex ideas and make the poem more engaging and memorable.

### Mood and Tone
The **mood** of a poem is the atmosphere or feeling it creates in the reader, while the **tone** is the poet's attitude toward the subject matter. A poem about a beautiful sunset might have a calm and peaceful mood, while the poet's tone could be one of wonder or nostalgia. Recognizing the difference between these two is key to fully understanding a poem's emotional impact.

### Rhyme and Rhythm
**Rhyme** is the repetition of similar sounds, usually at the end of lines, which gives poetry a musical quality. **Rhythm** is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables that creates a poem's beat. Together, they form the musical backbone of a poem, influencing how it is read and how it feels to the listener.

## Example
In a poem describing a storm, a poet might use personification by saying "the wind howled in anger," giving the wind human emotion. They could use auditory imagery with "the thunder roared like a lion" and tactile imagery with "the cold rain lashed against my skin." The mood might be one of fear and tension, while the tone could be dramatic and intense.

## Quick Revision
- Poetry uses aesthetic language to express feelings and ideas.
- Imagery appeals to the five senses to create vivid mental pictures.
- Figures of speech like metaphors and similes are used for special effects.
- Mood is the feeling created for the reader; tone is the poet's attitude.
- Rhyme and rhythm give poetry its musical quality and structure.
- Always read the poem slowly to understand its meaning and emotion.
- Look for repeated words or phrases as they often hold the key theme.
- Connect the poem's theme to your own experiences for better understanding.

## Exam Tips
- Read the poem at least twice before attempting any questions; first for general understanding, and second to analyze specific devices.
- When asked about poetic devices, don't just name them; explain their effect on the reader with a short example from the text.
- For questions on theme or mood, always support your answer with evidence from the poem, quoting relevant lines.
- Pay close attention to the title, as it often provides a crucial clue to the poem's central idea or theme.

notes.title: Vocabulary & Usage — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Introduction
Building a strong vocabulary is like sharpening the tools in your mental workshop. It's essential not just for scoring well in your English exams, but for expressing your thoughts clearly and powerfully in all walks of life.

### Word Power: More Than Just Meanings
A rich vocabulary isn't just about knowing a lot of words; it's about understanding their **nuances**, their subtle differences in meaning and feeling. For example, "happy," "content," "joyful," and "elated" all describe positive emotions, but each carries a different intensity and context. Mastering this difference is key to using language precisely.

### Context is King
The meaning of a word is often shaped by the words around it. This is called **context**. A word like "light" can mean not heavy, or it can refer to illumination. To understand a word correctly, you must always look at the sentence it's in. This is why reading widely is one of the best ways to improve your vocabulary.

### Word Families: Growing Your Vocabulary
Instead of learning single words, think in terms of **word families**. When you learn a new word like "decide," you can also learn its related forms: "decision," "decisive," "undecided," and "indecisively." This way, you multiply your vocabulary skills exponentially and understand how words are built.

### The Art of Usage
Knowing a word's definition is only half the battle. You must also know how to use it correctly in a sentence. This includes understanding what kind of words it usually pairs with (its **collocations**). You don't "make a decision," you "make a decision," but you "reach a decision." Using words in their natural partnerships makes your language sound more fluent and authentic.

### From Passive to Active
Reading helps you build a **passive vocabulary**—words you recognize. To truly own a word, you need to move it to your **active vocabulary**, which means you can use it confidently in your own writing and speech. The best way to do this is to practice using new words in your daily work, like in essays or diary entries.

### Example
Imagine you read the sentence, "The **meticulous** student checked her project three times." If you don't know "meticulous," you can guess its meaning from the context. The student is being very careful and precise. Now, let's use it actively: "For the science experiment, it was important to be meticulous in measuring the chemicals."

## Quick Revision
- Vocabulary is about precise word choice, not just knowing many words.
- Always determine a word's meaning from its surrounding context.
- Learn words in families (e.g., act, action, active, activity) to expand quickly.
- Correct usage involves knowing which words naturally go together (collocations).
- Aim to move words from your passive (recognizable) to active (usable) vocabulary.
- A strong vocabulary improves both exam scores and real-world communication.
- Reading is the most effective way to naturally acquire new words.
- Use a thesaurus to find synonyms, but always check their specific meanings.

## Exam Tips
- When answering vocabulary questions, read the entire sentence first before choosing a word. The context is your biggest clue.
- In writing sections, avoid repeating the same words. Use a thesaurus to find better synonyms, but be sure they fit the tone and meaning perfectly.
- Don't just memorize word lists. Learn words in context by reading stories, articles, and newspapers.
- Pay special attention to **phrasal verbs** and **idioms**, as they are high-frequency questions and are often used to test your practical understanding of the language.

notes.title: Structure of Atom — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Introduction
Understanding the structure of the atom is the absolute cornerstone of modern chemistry. It forms the basis for everything we learn about chemical bonding, reactions, and the properties of matter, making it a high-weightage chapter in your exams.

### Subatomic Particles
An atom is not an indivisible sphere but a complex entity made up of three fundamental particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons. Protons carry a positive charge and are found in the nucleus, the dense core of the atom. Neutrons are neutral particles, also residing in the nucleus, which add to its mass and stability. Electrons, which are much lighter and carry a negative charge, orbit the nucleus in specific regions called shells or orbitals.

### Atomic Models
Our understanding of the atom has evolved through several key models. **Thomson's Plum Pudding Model** pictured the atom as a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded within it. **Rutherford's Nuclear Model**, based on his famous gold foil experiment, established that the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus with electrons orbiting around it. However, this model couldn't explain why electrons didn't collapse into the nucleus. This was resolved by **Bohr's Model**, which introduced the idea of electrons existing in fixed, energy-level orbits or shells, absorbing or emitting energy when they jump between these levels.

### Quantum Mechanical Model
The Bohr model was a stepping stone, but the modern understanding is the **Quantum Mechanical Model**. This model describes electrons not as particles in fixed paths but as clouds of probability found in regions called **orbitals**. An orbital is a three-dimensional space where there is a high probability of finding an electron. These orbitals are defined by a set of four quantum numbers: the principal quantum number (n), the azimuthal quantum number (l), the magnetic quantum number (m), and the spin quantum number (s).

### Electron Configuration
The arrangement of electrons in the orbitals of an atom is known as its electron configuration. This arrangement follows a set of rules, most importantly the **Aufbau Principle**, which states that electrons fill the lowest energy orbitals first. The **Pauli Exclusion Principle** dictates that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers. Finally, **Hund's Rule** says that electrons will fill degenerate orbitals (orbitals of the same energy) singly before any pairing occurs. This configuration determines an element's chemical properties.

### Quantum Numbers
Quantum numbers are like an address for each electron in an atom. The **Principal Quantum Number (n)** indicates the main energy level or shell (n = 1, 2, 3...). The **Azimuthal Quantum Number (l)** defines the shape of the subshell (s, p, d, f). The **Magnetic Quantum Number (m)** specifies the orientation of a particular orbital in space. The **Spin Quantum Number (s)** describes the intrinsic spin of the electron, which can be either +½ or -½.

## Example
Let's write the electron configuration for Sodium (Na), which has an atomic number of 11. Following the Aufbau Principle, we fill the orbitals in order of increasing energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p... The 1s orbital holds 2 electrons, the 2s holds 2, and the 2p holds 6. After filling these first three orbitals (2+2+6=10 electrons), we have one electron left. This last electron goes into the next available orbital, which is the 3s. Therefore, the electron configuration for Sodium is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.

## Quick Revision
- Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
- Rutherford's experiment revealed a small, dense nucleus.
- Electrons occupy specific energy levels (shells) in the Bohr model.
- The Quantum Model describes electrons in probabilistic orbitals.
- Electron configuration follows rules like Aufbau and Hund's Rule.
- Quantum numbers define the unique address of each electron.

## Exam Tips
- Always start writing from the basic atomic structure and build up to quantum numbers for a logical flow in answers.
- Draw clear diagrams of the atomic models (Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr) and label all parts correctly; these are high-scoring visuals.
- Memorize the order of orbital filling (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d...) to write electron configurations quickly and accurately.
- Pay special attention to exceptions in electron configuration, like Chromium and Copper, as questions on these are common.
- Define all key terms like orbital, quantum number, and subshell precisely to secure marks for definitions.
keyPoints: Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
Rutherford's experiment revealed a small, dense nucleus.
Electrons occupy specific energy levels (shells) in the Bohr model.
The Quantum Model describes electrons in probabilistic orbitals.
Electron configuration follows rules like Aufbau and Hund's Rule.
Quantum numbers define the unique address of each electron.

notes.title: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Introduction
This chapter is the cornerstone of your entire chemistry journey, laying the fundamental language and tools you'll use to understand every other topic. Mastering these basic concepts is crucial not only for scoring well in exams but also for building a strong foundation for advanced chemical principles.

### Matter and its Classification
At its core, chemistry is the study of matter, which is anything that has mass and occupies space. We can broadly categorize matter based on its composition. A pure substance has a fixed composition and distinct properties, and it can be either an element, which cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means, or a compound, which is formed when two or more elements combine in a fixed ratio. On the other hand, a mixture consists of two or more substances that are physically combined, meaning they can be separated by physical processes like filtration or distillation, and they retain their individual properties.

### Laws of Chemical Combination
Chemists have discovered several fundamental laws that govern how substances react and combine. The Law of Conservation of Mass states that in a chemical reaction, matter is neither created nor destroyed; the total mass of the reactants is always equal to the total mass of the products. The Law of Definite Proportions tells us that a pure compound always contains the same elements combined in the same proportion by mass. Finally, the Law of Multiple Proportions explains that when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio.

### The Mole Concept
The mole concept is the bridge between the microscopic world of atoms and molecules and the macroscopic world of grams and liters that we can measure. One mole of any substance is defined as the amount that contains exactly 6.022 × 10²³ elementary entities, which could be atoms, molecules, ions, or other particles. This specific number is known as Avogadro's number. The mole is the central unit for quantifying the amount of a substance and allows us to perform stoichiometric calculations with ease.

### Stoichiometry and Calculations
Stoichiometry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the quantitative relationships between reactants and products in a chemical reaction. Using balanced chemical equations, we can determine the exact amounts of reactants needed or products formed. The key to solving these problems is understanding the mole ratio derived from the coefficients in the balanced equation. We often use the formula `Number of moles = Mass / Molar Mass` to convert between the mass of a substance and the number of moles.

### Concentration of Solutions
In chemistry, we often work with solutions, which are homogeneous mixtures of a solute (the substance being dissolved) and a solvent (the substance doing the dissolving). The concentration of a solution refers to the amount of solute present in a given amount of solution. The most common unit of concentration is molarity, which is defined as the number of moles of solute per liter of solution. It is expressed as `M = Moles of solute / Volume of solution (in litres)`.

## Example
Let's calculate the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 11.7 grams of sodium chloride (NaCl) in enough water to make 500 mL of solution.
1.  First, find the molar mass of NaCl: Na (23 g/mol) + Cl (35.5 g/mol) = 58.5 g/mol.
2.  Next, calculate the number of moles of NaCl: Moles = Mass / Molar Mass = 11.7 g / 58.5 g/mol = 0.2 moles.
3.  Convert the volume of the solution from milliliters to liters: 500 mL = 0.5 L.
4.  Finally, calculate the molarity: M = Moles / Volume (L) = 0.2 moles / 0.5 L = 0.4 M.

## Quick Revision
-   Matter is anything with mass and volume; classified as pure substances (elements/compounds) or mixtures.
-   **Law of Conservation of Mass**: Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.
-   One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles; its mass in grams is the atomic/molecular mass.
-   A **mole** is the SI unit for the amount of a substance.
-   **Stoichiometry** uses mole ratios from balanced equations for reaction calculations.
-   **Molarity (M)** is moles of solute per liter of solution.
-   The percentage composition of a compound is the mass percent of each element in it.
-   Empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound.

## Exam Tips
-   Always start stoichiometry problems by writing and **balancing the chemical equation** correctly; an unbalanced equation will lead to wrong answers.
-   Pay close attention to units in calculations, especially when converting between grams, moles, and liters. A common mistake is forgetting to convert mL to L for molarity.
-   Memorize the definitions and formulas for key terms like molarity, mole, and Avogadro's number, as they are frequently asked in one-word or one-sentence questions.
-   Practice problems involving the **Law of Multiple Proportions** thoroughly, as they test your understanding of the concept rather than just a simple calculation.

notes.title: Polynomials — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Polynomials form the building blocks of algebra and are fundamental to solving a vast array of problems in higher mathematics. Mastering this chapter is crucial as it lays the groundwork for understanding more complex functions and is frequently tested in board exams, often forming the basis for multi-mark questions.

### What is a Polynomial?
A polynomial is an algebraic expression made up of variables and constants, where the variables have only whole number exponents. Think of it as a mathematical phrase where numbers and letters are combined using addition, subtraction, and multiplication. The key rule is that the variable (usually 'x') cannot be in the denominator or have a fractional or negative exponent.

### Degree of a Polynomial
The degree of a polynomial is the highest power of the variable present in the expression. It's like identifying the most senior term in the expression. For example, in the polynomial 3x² - 5x + 2, the term with the highest power is 3x², so the degree of this polynomial is 2. This number tells us a lot about the shape of the graph the polynomial will make.

### Types of Polynomials Based on Degree
We classify polynomials based on their degree, giving them special names. A polynomial of degree 1 is called a **linear polynomial** (e.g., 2x + 3). A polynomial of degree 2 is a **quadratic polynomial** (e.g., x² - 4). And a polynomial of degree 3 is known as a **cubic polynomial** (e.g., 4x³ - x). Knowing these names helps us quickly understand the complexity of the equation we're dealing with.

### Zeroes (or Roots) of a Polynomial
The zeroes or roots of a polynomial are the values of the variable that make the polynomial equal to zero. If you have a polynomial expression like p(x), finding its zeroes means solving the equation p(x) = 0. These zeroes are incredibly important because they represent the points where the graph of the polynomial crosses the x-axis. For a quadratic equation, there can be a maximum of two zeroes.

### Relationship Between Zeroes and Coefficients
There's a beautiful and very useful relationship between the sum and product of the zeroes of a polynomial and its coefficients. For a quadratic polynomial in the form ax² + bx + c, the sum of its zeroes (let's call them α and β) is given by -b/a, and their product is c/a. This relationship allows us to find the sum and product of the roots without even knowing what the roots are!

### Example
Let's take the quadratic polynomial 2x² - 5x + 3. Here, a = 2, b = -5, and c = 3. The sum of its zeroes (α + β) will be -b/a = -(-5)/2 = 5/2. The product of its zeroes (αβ) will be c/a = 3/2. This means if we were to find the actual roots, their sum would be 2.5 and their product would be 1.5.

## Quick Revision
- A polynomial has variables with only whole number exponents.
- The highest power of the variable is the **degree** of the polynomial.
- A polynomial of degree 2 is **quadratic**, and its graph is a parabola.
- The **zeroes** of a polynomial are the x-values where the expression equals zero.
- For a quadratic ax² + bx + c, sum of zeroes = -b/a and product of zeroes = c/a.
- A polynomial of degree 'n' can have a maximum of 'n' zeroes.

## Exam Tips
- Always write the polynomial in standard form (descending powers of x) before finding its degree or zeroes.
- Remember the sign convention for the sum of zeroes (-b/a), it's a common place to make a mistake.
- If a question asks you to form a polynomial with given zeroes, use the sum and product formulas to find its coefficients.
- Practice factorising quadratic polynomials thoroughly, as it's the most direct method to find their zeroes and is essential for solving related word problems.
keyPoints: A polynomial has variables with only whole number exponents.
The highest power of the variable is the **degree** of the polynomial.
A polynomial of degree 2 is **quadratic**, and its graph is a parabola.
The **zeroes** of a polynomial are the x-values where the expression equals zero.
For a quadratic ax² + bx + c, sum of zeroes = -b/a and product of zeroes = c/a.
A polynomial of degree 'n' can have a maximum of 'n' zeroes.

notes.title: Polynomials — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Polynomials form the building blocks of algebra and are essential for solving complex equations. Mastering this chapter is crucial because it lays the foundation for understanding functions, graphs, and advanced mathematical concepts you'll encounter in higher classes.

### Understanding Polynomials
A polynomial is an algebraic expression that consists of variables and coefficients, involving only the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and non-negative integer exponents of variables. For example, 3x² - 2x + 5 is a polynomial, whereas 2x⁻¹ + 3 is not because it has a negative exponent.

### Degree of a Polynomial
The degree of a polynomial is the highest power of the variable present in the expression. It tells us about the polynomial's most significant term. For instance, in the polynomial 4x³ + 2x² - x + 7, the degree is 3 because the highest power of x is 3.

### Types of Polynomials Based on Degree
Polynomials are classified based on their degree. A polynomial of degree 1 is called a linear polynomial (e.g., 2x + 3), degree 2 is a quadratic polynomial (e.g., x² - 5x + 6), and degree 3 is a cubic polynomial (e.g., x³ + 2x² - x - 2).

### Zeroes of a Polynomial
The zeroes of a polynomial are the values of the variable for which the polynomial's value becomes zero. These are also known as roots or solutions. For the polynomial x² - 4, the zeroes are 2 and -2, because when you substitute these values for x, the expression equals zero.

### Factor Theorem
The Factor Theorem states that if a polynomial p(x) has a zero at x = a, then (x - a) is a factor of p(x). This is a powerful tool for factorizing polynomials. For example, if we know that 2 is a zero of p(x) = x² - 5x + 6, then (x - 2) must be a factor of the polynomial.

### Relationship Between Zeroes and Coefficients
For a quadratic polynomial in the form ax² + bx + c, the sum of the zeroes is equal to -b/a, and the product of the zeroes is equal to c/a. This relationship helps in finding the zeroes of a polynomial without solving the equation completely.

**Example:**
Consider the polynomial p(x) = 2x² - 8x + 6. Using the relationship, the sum of the zeroes should be -(-8)/2 = 4, and the product should be 6/2 = 3. If we factorize it, we get 2(x - 1)(x - 3), so the zeroes are 1 and 3. Indeed, 1 + 3 = 4 and 1 × 3 = 3.

## Quick Revision
- A polynomial has variables with non-negative integer exponents.
- The degree is the highest power of the variable.
- Linear, quadratic, and cubic are names for polynomials of degrees 1, 2, and 3.
- Zeroes are the values of x that make the polynomial equal to zero.
- The Factor Theorem connects zeroes to factors of the polynomial.
- For a quadratic, sum of zeroes = -b/a and product = c/a.

## Exam Tips
- Always write the polynomial in standard form (descending powers of x) before identifying its degree or finding zeroes.
- Remember the difference between a polynomial and an algebraic expression; not all expressions are polynomials.
- When using the Factor Theorem, clearly state that 'a' is a zero, hence (x - a) is a factor.
- Practice factorizing various polynomials, as this is a common question and forms the basis for finding zeroes.
- For word problems, first translate the given situation into a polynomial equation before solving it.

notes.title: अपठित गद्यांश (Unseen Passage) — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## अपठित गद्यांश के लिए तैयारी
अपठित गद्यांश प्रश्नों का अध्याय आपकी पढ़ने की समझ, तर्क करने की क्षमता और भाषा का ज्ञान दोनों की परीक्षा लेता है। इस अध्याय में दिए गए अंकों का वजन अक्सर अधिक होता है, इसलिए इस पर अच्छी तैयारी करना बहुत जरूरी है।

## मुख्य अवधारणाएँ
### पढ़ने की तकनीक
अपठित गद्यांश को पढ़ते समय सबसे पहले उसे ध्यान से और शांत से पढ़ें। पूरे अंश को एक बार पढ़ने के बाद उसका सार यह निकालें कि लेखक क्या बता रहा है। इससे आपको पूरे अंश का सही अर्थ समझने में मदद मिलेगी और आप बाद के प्रश्नों का जवाब आसानी से दे पाएंगे।

### प्रश्नों का विश्लेषण
प्रश्न पत्र में आने वाले प्रश्न आमतौर पर तीन प्रकार के होते हैं: पहले प्रश्न गद्यांश से सीधे उद्धृत शब्दों से संबंधित होते हैं, दूसरे प्रश्न गद्यांश के आधार पर तार्किक उत्तर मांगते हैं और तीसरे प्रश्न आपसे अपने विचार या अनुभव से जुड़ा उत्तर देने को कहते हैं। प्रत्येक प्रश्न को ध्यान से पढ़कर ही उसका उत्तर दें।

### शब्दार्थ और वाक्यांश
गद्यांश में आने वाले कठिन शब्दों और वाक्यांशों का अर्थ समझना बहुत जरूरी है। यदि कोई शब्द आपको नहीं पता है तो उसका अर्थ उस शब्द के आसपास के वाक्यों के आधार पर अनुमान लगाएं। अक्सर लेखक ही उस शब्द के अर्थ को समझाने का प्रयास करता है। इस तरह आप उस शब्द का सही अर्थ निकाल सकते हैं।

### उत्तर लेखन
उत्तर लिखते समय सबसे जरूरी बात है कि आपका उत्तर संक्षिप्त और स्पष्ट हो। प्रश्न के अनुसार उत्तर दें। लंबे-चौड़े उत्तर लिखने से न जाएं, बल्कि बिंदुवार तरीके से उत्तर लिखना बेहतर होता है। उत्तर में अपने विचार न दें, बल्कि गद्यांश के आधार पर ही उत्तर दें।

## उदाहरण
यदि प्रश्न है - "लेखक क्या कहता है कि पुस्तकें हमें कैसे मार्गदर्शन करती हैं?" तो आपका उत्तर इस प्रकार होना चाहिए: "लेखक कहता है कि पुस्तकें हमारे अंदर छुपे हुए गुणों को उजागर करती हैं और हमें सही राह दिखाती हैं।" यहाँ आपने सीधे गद्यांश का हवाला दिया है और उत्तर संक्षिप्त दिया है।

## त्वरित समीक्षा
- गद्यांश को शांत से पढ़ें और उसका सार निकालें।
- प्रश्नों को ध्यान से पढ़ें और समझें कि वह क्या पूछ रहे हैं।
- कठिन शब्दों का अर्थ गद्यांश के आधार पर अनुमान लगाएं।
- उत्तर संक्षिप्त और गद्यांश से संबंधित दें।
- उत्तर में अपने व्यक्तिगत विचार न दें।
- गलत वर्तनी और व्याकरण से बचें।
- समय का ध्यान रखते हुए प्रश्नों का उत्तर दें।

## परीक्षा सलाह
- अपठित गद्यांश के प्रश्नों को हमेशा पहले हल करें क्योंकि ये अंकों में आसानी से अंक ला सकते हैं।
- जब आप प्रश्न का उत्तर दे रहे हों तो उस शब्द को बोल्ड या अंडरलाइन न करें, जिसे प्रश्न में दिया गया हो।
- वैसे प्रश्न जिनके लिए लंबे उत्तर की आवश्यकता हो, उन्हें अंत में हल करें।
- अपने उत्तर को पढ़कर जांच लें कि आपने पूरा प्रश्न हल कर दिया है या नहीं।

notes.title: Reading Comprehension — Revision Notes
notes.content:
## Introduction
Mastering reading comprehension is the single most important skill for your English exams and beyond. It forms the foundation for answering questions accurately, understanding complex texts, and developing critical thinking abilities that you'll use throughout your academic career.

### Understanding the Passage
Reading comprehension isn't just about reading words; it's about understanding the **meaning, purpose, and tone** of a written piece. Before you jump into answering questions, take a moment to grasp the central idea or theme of the text. Ask yourself: What is the author trying to say? Who is the target audience? This initial understanding will guide you through the entire process.

### Active Reading Techniques
Don't just pass your eyes over the text. Engage with it by **highlighting key points**, making notes in the margins, and summarizing paragraphs in your own mind. This active approach helps you retain information better and locate specific details quickly when you're answering questions. It turns a passive activity into an interactive learning experience.

### Decoding Questions
Every question in a comprehension test is a clue. Pay close attention to the **exact wording** of each question. Words like "not," "main," "infer," and "according to the text" completely change what is being asked. Learning to identify these keywords is like learning to follow a map; it ensures you're heading in the right direction with your answer.

### Structuring Your Answers
A well-structured answer is often the difference between a good and an excellent score. Start by directly addressing the question in your first sentence. Then, support your answer with **specific evidence or quotes** from the passage. Finally, conclude with a sentence that reinforces your point, showing the examiner that you've understood the connection between your reasoning and the text.

### Inferring and Analyzing
Some questions won't have direct answers in the text. They will ask you to **infer** or deduce information based on what is implied. This requires you to read between the lines, understand character motivations, or predict outcomes. This skill shows a deeper level of comprehension and is often where students can score extra marks by demonstrating critical thinking.

## Example
Imagine a passage describes a character who is always looking out the window during a storm, but never goes outside. A question might ask, "What can you infer about the character's feelings?" A good answer wouldn't just say "sad." It would infer that the character might feel **trapped or long for freedom**, connecting their internal state to their external actions described in the text.

## Quick Revision
- Always read the passage twice: once for general understanding, once for details.
- Underline or highlight the main idea and supporting arguments.
- Analyze the question keywords carefully before formulating an answer.
- Use direct quotes from the text to support your points.
- Structure your answer with a clear topic sentence and supporting evidence.
- For inference questions, base your answer on clues in the text, not personal opinions.

## Exam Tips
- **Manage your time wisely**. Don't spend too long on one question; move on and come back if needed.
- **Write in complete sentences**, even for short answer questions, to ensure clarity and full marks.
- **Avoid copying large chunks** of the text; instead, paraphrase and integrate evidence into your own sentences.
- Pay special attention to **vocabulary-in-context** questions, as they test your ability to understand words based on surrounding text.

notes.title: Solutions — Revision Notes
notes.content:
# Solutions — Revision Notes

## Introduction
Solutions is the first physical-chemistry chapter of Class 12 and a favourite for numericals: concentration terms, Raoult's law, colligative properties and their anomalies (abnormal molar mass) together account for 5-7 board marks.

## Key Concepts

### Types & concentration terms
Binary solutions have solute + solvent. Key expressions: molarity M = mol solute/L solution (temperature-dependent); molality m = mol solute/kg solvent (temperature-independent); mole fraction x; parts per million for trace amounts. Know when each is preferred.

### Solubility ideas
"Like dissolves like": polar solvents dissolve polar solutes. Gases dissolve less as temperature rises but more under high pressure — **Henry's law**: p = K_H x. High K_H means low solubility; this law explains soda fizzing out when opened and the bends in scuba divers.

### Raoult's law
Vapour pressure of a component = mole fraction × pure-component vapour pressure: p₁ = x₁ p₁°. Ideal solutions obey it across all ranges (benzene–toluene). Positive deviation (A–B attractions weaker) gives higher p than ideal; negative deviation (stronger A–B, e.g. acetone+chloroform) gives lower p. Azeotropes boil at constant composition and cannot be split by simple distillation.

### Colligative properties
Depend only on the NUMBER of solute particles: (1) relative lowering of vapour pressure, (2) elevation of boiling point ΔT_b = K_b·m, (3) depression of freezing point ΔT_f = K_f·m, (4) osmotic pressure π = CRT (best for polymers/proteins). These give molar masses; isotonic solutions have equal π.

### Abnormal molar mass
Dissociation (NaCl → 2 particles) makes properties larger → observed molar mass lower. Association (benzoic acid dimerises in benzene) does the reverse. The **van't Hoff factor** i = normal molar mass / abnormal molar mass corrects every colligative formula.

## Example
0.1 m NaCl solution: i ≈ 2, so effective particle molality = 0.2 m. Its freezing point drops about twice as much as 0.1 m glucose (i = 1) — dissociation doubles the particle count, not the moles.

## Quick Revision
- Molality & mole fraction don't change with temperature; molarity does.
- Henry: p = K_H x — higher K_H, less soluble gas.
- Ideal solution obeys Raoult at every composition.
- Colligative = "count of particles", not their identity.
- π = CRT; isotonic solutions share equal osmotic pressure.
- i > 1 dissociation, i < 1 association, i = 1 ideal nonelectrolyte.
- ΔT_f and ΔT_b scale with molality × i.

## Exam Tips
- State units of K_b, K_f and K_H — numericals lose marks on unit slips.
- Write "i = 2 (assuming complete dissociation)" before NaCl/CaCl₂ calculations.
- Choose osmotic pressure for macromolecules: other methods need large measurable amounts.
- In deviation questions, first compare A–B attraction strength with A–A and B–B.
- Practise interconversion of molarity ↔ molality using density; it appears every few years.

notes.title: Principles of Inheritance and Variation — Revision Notes
notes.content:
# Principles of Inheritance and Variation — Revision Notes

## Introduction
This genetics chapter carries one of the highest weightages in Class 12 biology. It builds from Mendel's pea experiments to chromosome theory, linkage, and human genetic disorders — conceptual clarity here also powers the Molecular Basis of Inheritance chapter.

## Key Concepts

### Mendel's laws
- **Law of Dominance**: in a monohybrid cross, only the dominant trait shows in F₁ (tall × dwarf → all tall).
- **Law of Segregation**: alleles separate cleanly during gamete formation; F₂ shows 3 : 1 phenotype and 1 : 2 : 1 genotype. This is the only law without exceptions among Mendel's three.
- **Law of Independent Assortment**: allele pairs for different traits separate independently in a dihybrid cross, giving the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 F₂ ratio. Valid only for genes on different chromosomes or far apart on the same one.

### Test cross & back cross
Test cross mates a dominant-phenotype individual with the recessive parent type: a 1 : 1 ratio reveals a heterozygote. It is the standard "find the genotype" tool.

### Incomplete & codominance
- Incomplete dominance: heterozygote is intermediate (snapdragon: red × white → pink, F₂ 1 : 2 : 1).
- Codominance: both alleles express together (AB blood group; ABO alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ codominant, i recessive).

### Chromosome theory & linkage
Sutton and Boveri united Mendel's factors with chromosomes. Genes on the same chromosome show **linkage**; recombinant frequency depends on distance (closer = fewer recombinants). Drosophila linkage maps came from these ratios.

### Sex determination & disorders
Humans: XX female, XY male; the father's gamete decides the child's sex. Mendelian disorders include haemophilia (X-linked recessive), sickle-cell anaemia (autosomal recessive codominant), phenylketonuria. Chromosomal disorders: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner's syndrome (XO female), Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY male).

## Example
Cross a carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) with a normal father (XᴴY) for haemophilia.
Gametes: Xᴴ, Xʰ × Xᴴ, Y → daughters: ½ carrier; sons: ½ affected. So 25% of children (only boys) are expected haemophiliacs.

## Quick Revision
- F₂ monohybrid: 3 : 1 phenotype, 1 : 2 : 1 genotype.
- Dihybrid F₂: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 needs independent assortment.
- Test cross reveals heterozygosity (1 : 1 result).
- Blood group AB shows codominance; pink snapdragon shows incomplete dominance.
- Recombination frequency ↑ with gene distance on a chromosome.
- Father determines the sex of the child in humans.
- Down = trisomy 21; Turner = XO; Klinefelter = XXY.

## Exam Tips
- Always draw a Punnett square with gametes labelled — it carries step marks.
- Name the ratio AND the law behind it when answering "identify the cross" questions.
- Keep a one-line mnemonic for chromosomal disorders: Down-21, Turner-XO, Klinefelter-XXY.
- In pedigree problems, eliminate X-linked recessive if father-to-son transmission appears.
- Practise writing gametes in one line before the square; most errors start there.

notes.title: Number Systems — Revision Notes
notes.content:
# Number Systems — Revision Notes

## Introduction
Number Systems extends your number family from rationals to the full real line: you classify numbers, meet irrational roots, and locate them on the number line. It is the base for every algebra chapter that follows.

## Key Concepts

### Number family
Natural (N) ⊂ whole (W) ⊂ integers (Z) ⊂ rational (Q) ⊂ real (R). Rationals are expressible as p/q (q ≠ 0); irrationals are not. Every real number has a unique position on the number line.

### Decimal expansions
Rational numbers give terminating decimals (7/8 = 0.875) or repeating decimals (1/3 = 0.333…). Irrational numbers give non-terminating, non-repeating decimals like √2 = 1.41421356… The q-test: p/q (lowest terms) terminates iff q = 2ᵐ5ⁿ.

### Irrational numbers
√2, √3, π, 0.101101110… are irrational. Key closure facts: sum/product of two irrationals **may** be rational (√2 × √2 = 2) — check, don't assume. Rational + irrational is always irrational.

### Locating √n on the number line
Spiral/semicircle construction: for √2, draw a right triangle with legs 1 and 1 (hypotenuse √2), transfer the length to the number line with a compass. Repeating with hypotenuse as a leg builds √3, √4, … — the "spiral of roots".

### Laws of exponents (real bases)
aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; a⁰ = 1 (a ≠ 0); a⁻ᵐ = 1/aᵐ. Fractional index n√a = a^(1/n), and a^(p/q) = (q√a)ᵖ. Rationalisation removes surds from denominators by multiplying with the conjugate.

## Example
Simplify (√5 + √3)(√5 − √3).
= (√5)² − (√3)² = 5 − 3 = 2. The conjugate pair turns surds into a clean rational — this pattern is asked repeatedly.

## Quick Revision
- p/q terminates ⇔ q has only 2s and 5s (lowest terms).
- Rational + irrational = always irrational.
- √2 × √2 = 2 shows irrational × irrational can be rational.
- √n construction: right triangle + compass transfer.
- a^(1/n) = nth root; a^(p/q) = q√(aᵖ).
- Rationalise by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

## Exam Tips
- For "classify the number" questions, show the p/q test or the non-repeating decimal argument, not just the label.
- Practise compass constructions neatly — construction marks carry marks.
- In rationalisation, conjugate of a + √b is a − √b; write both multiplications.
- Convert recurring decimals to fractions with 10ˣ/9…9 subtraction once; it reappears in Class 10.
- Never write √(a+b) = √a + √b — it is wrong; expand squares instead.

√2 × √2 = 2 shows irrational × irrational can be rational.
√n construction: right triangle + compass transfer.

notes.title: Sets — Revision Notes
notes.content:
# Sets — Revision Notes

## Introduction
Sets is the language of Class 11 mathematics: every later topic (functions, probability, relations) is written in set notation. The chapter is mostly notation and logic, making it one of the easiest scoring chapters if you know the laws cold.

## Key Concepts

### Representing sets
A set is a well-defined collection. Roster form lists elements {2, 4, 6}; set-builder form describes a rule {x : x = 2n, n ∈ N, 1 ≤ n ≤ 3}. Order and repetition don't matter: {1, 2} = {2, 1, 1}.

### Types of sets
Empty set ∅ (no elements), singleton (one element), finite and infinite sets, equal sets (same elements), equivalent sets (same number/cardinality of elements). Note: ∅ has 0 elements but {∅} has 1.

### Subsets and power set
A ⊆ B if every element of A lies in B. Every set has 2ⁿ subsets (n = number of elements) and 2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets. Intervals like [a, b], (a, b) are subsets of R written in interval notation.

### Venn diagrams & operations
Union A ∪ B (in A or B), intersection A ∩ B (in both), difference A − B (in A, not B), complement A′ (in U, not A). Venn diagrams turn set problems into picture-counting problems — always draw them.

### Laws
- De Morgan: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.
- Distributive: A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C); dual with ∩/∪ swapped.
- Idempotent, commutative, associative laws hold for ∪ and ∩.

### Cardinality formula
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
Three sets: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A)+n(B)+n(C) − n(A∩B) − n(B∩C) − n(A∩C) + n(A∩B∩C). This is the engine of every "survey/inclusion-exclusion" word problem.

## Example
In a class, 40 like maths, 25 like physics, 12 like both. How many like at least one subject?
n(M ∪ P) = 40 + 25 − 12 = 53 students.

## Quick Revision
- 2ⁿ subsets, 2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets for an n-element set.
- {∅} ≠ ∅; {0} is a singleton, not empty.
- De Morgan's two laws swap ∪↔∩ with a complement.
- n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
- Equivalent sets have equal cardinality; equal sets are identical.
- Complement is always taken relative to the universal set U.

## Exam Tips
- Write the law you are applying before each simplification step in proofs.
- For word problems, define sets with letters first (let M = students who like maths…).
- Draw a three-circle Venn diagram with the innermost overlap filled first.
- Watch words: "only maths" means n(A) − n(A ∩ B), not n(A).
- Check subset questions for the empty set and the set itself — both always count.

notes.title: Electric Charges and Fields — Revision Notes
notes.content:
# Electric Charges and Fields — Revision Notes

## Introduction
This chapter opens electrostatics: how charges behave at rest, the fields they create, and Gauss's law — the fastest tool for symmetric charge distributions. Boards regularly take 5-7 marks from here, including one derivation.

## Key Concepts

### Charge basics
Charge is quantised: q = ne, with e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. It is conserved in every isolated system and additive with sign. Like charges repel, unlike attract. Conductors let charges flow; insulators hold them fixed; charging by induction moves charge without contact.

### Coulomb's law
F = k q₁q₂/r², with k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N m²/C². The force acts along the line joining the point charges, obeys Newton's third law, and is valid for point charges. In a medium of dielectric constant K, the force divides by K.

### Electric field
E = F/q₀ (force per unit positive test charge), unit N/C or V/m. Field of a point charge: E = kq/r², radially outward for positive q. Field lines start on + and end on − charges, never cross, and their density shows strength.

### Electric dipole
Two equal, opposite charges separated by 2a. Dipole moment p = q × 2a, directed from − to +. Axial field: E = 2kp/r³; equatorial field: E = kp/r³ (opposite to p). Torque in uniform field: τ = pE sinθ. Net force on a dipole in a uniform field is zero.

### Gauss's law
Total flux through a closed surface Φ = q(enclosed)/ε₀. Flux counts field lines; charges outside contribute zero net flux. Standard results: infinite wire → E = λ/(2πε₀r); infinite sheet → E = σ/(2ε₀) (independent of distance); charged spherical shell → outside like a point charge, inside E = 0.

## Example
Two +2 μC charges sit 3 cm apart in air. Field at the midpoint?
Each charge is 1.5 cm = 0.015 m away; fields are equal and opposite → E = 0. Point-charge symmetry kills the field at the centre of two equal like charges.

## Quick Revision
- q = ne; e is the smallest free charge.
- Coulomb force in medium drops by factor K.
- E is force per unit test charge, pointing away from + charge.
- Field lines never intersect; they are dense where E is strong.
- Dipole: axial 2kp/r³, equatorial kp/r³, τ = pE sinθ.
- Gauss: Φ = q(in)/ε₀ — only enclosed charge matters.
- Inside a conductor/shell, electrostatic field is zero.

## Exam Tips
- State all symbols and units in derivations — step marking checks them.
- Use Gauss's law only when symmetry exists (sphere, wire, sheet); otherwise fall back to Coulomb summation.
- Draw the field-line diagram; labelled diagrams earn marks even in numericals.
- Memorise the three Gauss results with their distance dependence (1/r², 1/r, constant).
- In dipole torque questions, specify the angle θ between p and E clearly.

Dipole: axial 2kp/r³, equatorial kp/r³, τ = pE sinθ.
Gauss: Φ = q(in)/ε₀ — only enclosed charge matters.
